Before you change a single word on a website, you need to know how Google finds pages, what the words of SEO mean, and which free tools you will use. This module gives you that foundation, with Nigerian small-business examples, and helps you set up your accounts safely.

**SEO** stands for **search engine optimisation**. It means making a website easier for search engines to find, understand and show to the right people, without paying for each click. When a woman in Ibadan types "tailor near Bodija" into Google, the businesses that appear first did not get there by luck. Their pages were found, understood and judged useful for that search.

Google explains its own system in a document called **How Search Works**. It describes three stages. Every page that ever appears in Google has passed through all three. If you understand these stages, you will know where to look when a page is not showing up.
A person standing beside a large search bar and results
Search engines collect pages first, then choose which ones to show for each search.
Stage 1: Crawling

Google uses automatic programs called **crawlers** (Google's is called **Googlebot**) to visit pages on the web. Crawlers find new pages mainly by following links from pages they already know, and from **sitemaps**, which are files that list a site's pages. If no other page links to your new page and you have not submitted a sitemap, Google may take a long time to find it, or may never find it.
Stage 2: Indexing

After crawling a page, Google tries to understand it: the text, headings, images, title and other signals. It then may store the page in the **Google index**, a huge database of pages. Not every crawled page is indexed. Pages that are copies of other pages, very thin, or blocked with a **noindex** instruction are usually left out.
Stage 3: Serving results

When someone searches, Google looks through its index for pages that match and returns the ones it thinks are most relevant and useful. Google says many factors are involved, including the searcher's location, language and device. That is why a search for "bakery" on a phone in Port Harcourt shows different results from the same search in Kano.

Worked example: Is the new page in Google?
For example, Ngozi runs a small chops business in Lekki, Lagos. Her web designer added a new page, ngozichops.com/party-packs, two weeks ago. She cannot find it on Google.
She types site:ngozichops.com into Google. This special search shows pages Google has indexed from her domain. She sees 6 results, but not the party packs page.
She types site:ngozichops.com/party-packs. No results. The page is not in the index yet.
She checks her home page and menu. Nothing links to the new page, so crawlers have no path to it.
She asks the designer to add a "Party Packs" link to the menu and to the home page, and to submit the sitemap in Google Search Console (Lesson 3 shows how).
Ten days later she repeats the site: search and the page appears.
The page was not being found because no links pointed to it. Adding internal links and a sitemap fixed the crawling stage, and indexing followed.

The site: search is useful for a fast look, but Google says it does not always show every indexed page. For an exact answer about one page, use the URL Inspection tool in Google Search Console.
Two instructions that are often confused

A file called **robots.txt** sits at the root of a site (for example example.com/robots.txt) and tells crawlers which areas they may not crawl. It controls crawling, not indexing. Google's documentation says a page blocked in robots.txt can still appear in results if other sites link to it. To keep a page out of Google, the page needs a **noindex** rule, and Googlebot must be able to crawl the page to see that rule. A common, costly mistake is a designer leaving "Discourage search engines" switched on in WordPress after building a site, which keeps the whole site out of results until someone notices.
What SEO can and cannot do
**You can control:** whether your pages can be crawled, what they say, how clearly they are written, how fast and mobile-friendly they are, and how your Google Business Profile looks.
**You can influence:** whether other trusted websites mention and link to you, and how many genuine reviews customers leave.

**You cannot control:** Google's ranking systems, competitors, or how many people search. Nobody can guarantee a number one position, and Google itself warns site owners to be careful of anyone who promises that.

Google publishes its rules for site owners in **Google Search Essentials**. It has three parts: technical requirements (what Google needs to crawl and show a page), spam policies (tricks that can get a site demoted or removed), and key best practices. Google also has a free **SEO Starter Guide** written for beginners. You will meet both throughout this course, and they are listed in the sources.

Keywords and search intent

A **keyword** (or **query**) is the word or phrase people type or speak into a search engine. "Ankara fabric" is a short keyword. "where to buy ankara fabric in Aba wholesale" is a **long-tail keyword**: longer, more specific, usually searched less often, but by people much closer to buying.
**Search intent** is the reason behind the search. Matching intent is one of the most important ideas in SEO, because Google tries to show pages that satisfy what the person actually wants.
Two kinds of searcher
Learning (informational)
Buying (transactional or local)
how to tie gele
what is shea butter good for
best fabric for hot weather
buy gele online Lagos
shea butter wholesale price Kano
tailor near me
The same topic can be searched to learn or to buy, and each needs a different kind of page.

Practitioners commonly group intent into four types: **informational** (wants to learn), **navigational** (wants a particular site, such as "Jumia login"), **commercial** (comparing options, such as "best blender under 50k") and **transactional or local** (ready to buy or visit). A how-to blog post suits informational intent. A product page or Google Business Profile suits transactional and local intent.
Worked example: Matching pages to intent
For example, Halima sells shea butter products from Kano and has a simple website. She lists five searches she cares about and decides which page should answer each.
"what is shea butter good for": informational. She plans a blog article explaining uses for skin and hair.
"raw shea butter wholesale Kano": transactional and local. Her wholesale page with prices per kg, minimum order and a WhatsApp button.
"Halima Shea Kano": navigational. Her home page and Google Business Profile should appear; no new page needed.
"shea butter vs cocoa butter": commercial and informational. A comparison article.
"shea butter shop near me": local. Her Google Business Profile with correct address and hours.
Five searches, four different page types. She now builds pages to fit intent instead of repeating the same keyword everywhere.
Links and authority

A **backlink** is a link from another website to yours. Google's documents describe links as one way it discovers pages and judges how relevant and trusted they are. One link from a respected Nigerian news site or trade association usually means far more than dozens of links from unrelated, low-quality sites. **Internal links** are links between pages on your own site; they help both visitors and crawlers move around. **Anchor text** is the clickable words of a link, and it should describe the page it points to, such as "wholesale shea butter prices" rather than "click here".
Three more words you will hear
**Ranking or position:** where a result appears on the page. Position 1 is the top organic result. Search Console reports an average position for each query.
**Impression:** one time your result was shown to a searcher, whether or not they clicked.
**Click-through rate (CTR):** clicks divided by impressions. If a page was shown 1,000 times and clicked 40 times, its CTR is 4 percent. You will use this in Module 3.

Your Google account holds the keys to every SEO tool, so secure it first.
Step 1: Secure the Google account

Use a business Google account rather than a personal one where possible. Turn on **2-Step Verification** in your Google Account security settings, so a stolen password alone cannot open it. Keep recovery phone numbers and email up to date. If the account is lost, so is access to years of Search Console data and the Business Profile.
Step 2: Add the site to Search Console
Go to search.google.com/search-console and sign in.

Choose a property type. A **Domain** property covers every version of the site (http, https, www and subdomains) but must be verified with a DNS record at your domain registrar. A **URL prefix** property covers one exact address, such as https://www.example.com.ng/, and offers more verification options.

Verify ownership. For URL prefix you can upload an HTML file, add a meta tag to the home page, or use an existing Google Analytics or Google Tag Manager connection. For Domain you copy a TXT record into the DNS settings at your registrar or host.
Open the **Sitemaps** report and submit your sitemap address. Many sites use /sitemap.xml; WordPress SEO plugins such as Yoast SEO or Rank Math create one for you.
Wait a few days for data to appear in the **Performance** report.
Worked example: Verifying a WordPress site on a phone
For example, Chioma manages the website for her church women's fellowship in Enugu. It runs on WordPress with the Yoast SEO plugin, and she has only a phone.
She chooses a URL prefix property and enters https://www.fellowshipenugu.org/ exactly as the site loads.
Search Console offers an HTML tag. She copies it.
In WordPress she opens Yoast SEO settings, finds the site connections area for Google verification, and pastes only the code part of the tag.
She returns to Search Console and taps Verify. It succeeds.
She submits sitemap_index.xml (the address Yoast shows) in the Sitemaps report and sees the status Success.
In about 20 minutes, without a laptop, the site is verified and Google has a list of its pages.
Step 3: Give access the right way

Never share your Google password with a designer, agency or volunteer. Search Console lets an owner add **users** with Full or Restricted permission under Settings, Users and permissions. Google Business Profile also lets you add managers. When someone stops working with you, remove their access the same day.

Common SEO scams

Be wary of messages promising "guaranteed number one on Google in 7 days", offers to sell thousands of backlinks or reviews, or emails claiming your site will be removed from Google unless you pay. Google's own advice on hiring an SEO says no one can guarantee a top ranking. Buying links or reviews breaks Google's policies and can harm your site.
Protect customer data

Search Console and Analytics show search and visit data, but if your site has contact forms, it may also collect names and phone numbers. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 expects organisations to tell people what personal data they collect and why. Add a simple privacy notice and keep form entries away from shared WhatsApp groups.
Step 4: Record a starting point

Before you change anything, write down where the site stands today. This is called a **baseline**. Without it you cannot prove that your work made a difference. Once Search Console has a few weeks of data, note the total clicks and impressions for the last 28 days, the top five queries, and how many pages the Pages report lists as indexed and not indexed. Run the home page through PageSpeed Insights on mobile and note the result. Save these numbers in a simple sheet with the date. In Module 3 you will compare against them.
With these tools set up, every change you make in the coming modules can be measured. That is what separates real SEO work from guessing.

**Seed words:** write 5 to 10 plain words for what the business sells, in the customer's language (including Pidgin or local names if customers use them).

Choosing between keywords

You will not have exact search numbers without paid tools, and that is fine. Judge each phrase on three questions. **Relevance:** does the business really offer what this searcher wants? **Intent:** is this person close to buying, or just learning? **Competition:** when you search it, are the top results giant national sites like Jumia and Wikipedia, or small local businesses like yours? A long-tail local phrase such as "birthday cake delivery Bodija" may bring fewer visitors than "birthday cake", but those visitors are far more likely to order.
Do not repeat the keyword everywhere

Filling a page with the same phrase again and again is called keyword stuffing. Google's spam policies list it as a violation. Use the main keyword naturally in the title, a heading and the opening text, then write normally using related words.

Also look at the businesses already ranking for your main phrases. Open the top three results and note what their pages include: prices, photos, delivery areas, FAQs. You are not copying them. You are learning what searchers expect to find, so your page can answer those needs more clearly and with local details only you can give.

Changing a URL safely

If you change a page address, set up a **301 redirect** from the old URL to the new one (most WordPress SEO plugins and hosting panels can do this). Otherwise visitors and Google following old links get a "page not found" error, and the page loses the value of links pointing to it.
Write the main content for people

The text on the page matters more than any tag. Answer the questions a customer would ask before buying: what it is, prices or price ranges, sizes, delivery areas, how long it takes, how to pay (for example by bank transfer, Paystack link or POS on delivery), and how to contact you. Use short paragraphs and lists so phone readers can scan. Put your phone number and a WhatsApp link (wa.me followed by the number in international format, such as wa.me/234...) where people can tap them easily.
Structured data, briefly

**Structured data** is extra code (usually in a format called JSON-LD) that labels information on a page, such as a business's name, address, opening hours or a product price, using the shared vocabulary at schema.org. Google can use it to show richer results. Many WordPress SEO plugins add basic structured data for you. You can check a page with Google's free **Rich Results Test**. It is useful, but it is not a replacement for clear content.

How Google ranks local results
Google's Business Profile help centre says local results are based mainly on three things:
**Relevance:** how well the profile matches the search. Complete, accurate categories and descriptions help.
**Distance:** how far the business is from the searcher or the place named in the search. You cannot change this, except by serving genuine areas honestly.
**Prominence:** how well known the business is, using information such as reviews, links and articles across the web. Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help.
Setting up the profile
Go to google.com/business and sign in with your business Google account. Search first to see if a profile already exists; if so, request access instead of creating a duplicate.
Enter the business name exactly as customers see it on your signboard, receipts and social pages. Do not add extra keywords or locations to the name; Google's guidelines forbid it.
Choose the most specific primary category (for example "Cake shop" rather than "Store"), then add a few accurate secondary categories.

Add your address if customers visit you. If you go to customers (such as a mobile mechanic or home cleaner), set it up as a service-area business and list the areas you serve, without showing a home address.
Add phone, WhatsApp-reachable number, website, opening hours and a description of what you offer.
Verify. Google decides which methods to offer, which may include phone or text, email, or recording a short video showing your signage and workspace.
Add real photos: shopfront, inside, products, team at work. Keep adding new ones over time.

SEO practitioners call your business name, address and phone number **NAP**. Keep them the same everywhere: your website footer, Business Profile, Facebook and Instagram pages, WhatsApp Business profile and any online business directories you are listed in. If one site says "Shop 12, Ikeja Computer Village" and another says an old address in Yaba, both customers and Google get confused.

Content Quality, Ethics and Measurement

Rankings that last come from helpful content on a healthy, fast site, built without tricks. This module teaches you to judge content the way Google's guidance describes, fix common technical problems, stay inside Google's spam policies, and measure results honestly in Search Console.

Google's guidance on **creating helpful, reliable, people-first content** says its ranking systems aim to reward content made mainly to help people, not content made mainly to rank in search engines. It offers self-assessment questions you can use on any page. Does the content give original information or analysis? Would someone leave feeling they learned enough to reach their goal? Would you trust it? Does it show first-hand experience?

Apply these questions honestly to your client's top pages. Many small-business pages fail simply because they say almost nothing: a heading, a photo and "Call us".
E-E-A-T in plain words

Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines, used by people who help Google evaluate its results, describe **E-E-A-T**: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trustworthiness. Trust is the most important. For a small business this means simple, real things: show who runs the business, where it is, real photos of your work, your contact details, honest prices and genuine customer reviews. A recipe page from a caterer who has cooked jollof for 300-guest weddings, with her own photos, shows experience that a copied article cannot.
What about AI writing tools?

Google has said that using AI to help create content is not against its guidelines in itself. What breaks its spam policies is producing many pages, by any method, mainly to manipulate rankings without adding value. If you use AI, check every fact, add your own experience and photos, and edit until it sounds like you.

Mobile first and page speed

Google uses **mobile-first indexing**: it mainly crawls and indexes the mobile version of a page. In Nigeria most of your visitors are also likely to be on phones, often on costly data. A slow, heavy page loses them. Google measures real-world experience with **Core Web Vitals**:
Metric
What it measures
Good threshold
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
How quickly the main content appears
2.5 seconds or less
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
How quickly the page responds to taps and clicks
200 milliseconds or less
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
How much the page jumps around while loading
0.1 or less

Check any page in **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev). It shows field data from real Chrome users when enough exists, and a lab test with specific suggestions. Search Console's **Core Web Vitals** report groups your pages as Good, Needs improvement or Poor.
Worked example: Making a fashion page load faster
For example, Ifeoma sells ready-to-wear Ankara dresses. Her collection page on mobile has an LCP of 6.8 seconds in PageSpeed Insights, and Search Console marks it Poor.
PageSpeed Insights lists "Properly size images". Her 24 product photos are straight from her phone, about 3 to 4 MB each.
She resizes each to 1200 pixels wide and saves as WebP, bringing each to roughly 150 KB. Total image weight drops from about 80 MB to about 3.6 MB.
She turns on lazy loading so photos lower down only load when the visitor scrolls.
She removes an auto-playing background video and an unused chat plugin.
She retests: mobile LCP is now 2.3 seconds.
The page moves into the Good range for LCP and costs visitors far less data. Image size was the main problem, which is very common on small business sites.
Common technical mistakes
**Noindex left on:** WordPress "Discourage search engines" ticked after launch. Check in Settings, Reading.
**Duplicate pages:** the same product at several URLs. Pick one and use a canonical tag or redirect.
**Broken links and 404 errors:** pages deleted without redirects. Search Console's Pages report shows "Not found (404)".
**No HTTPS:** sites without an SSL certificate show "Not secure" in Chrome. Most Nigerian and international hosts offer free certificates through Let's Encrypt.
**Thin pages:** dozens of near-empty tag or category pages. Improve them or keep them out of the index.

Fix problems in order of impact. A noindex on the whole site or a broken home page is an emergency. Slow product images on your best-selling page come next. A few 404 errors on old blog posts nobody visits can wait. Write each issue in your sheet with the page, the problem, the fix and the date fixed, so you can show the work later in your audit.
Read the Pages report calmly

Search Console's Pages report always shows some pages as "not indexed". That is normal for redirects, duplicates and pages you chose to exclude. Worry only when an important page you want in Google appears there, and use URL Inspection to see why.

Some SEO sellers promise fast results through tricks. These tactics break **Google's spam policies**, part of Search Essentials. Google says sites that violate them may rank lower or not appear at all, either through automated systems or a **manual action** by a Google reviewer. When that happens, the business loses the free traffic it depended on. Ethical SEO protects your clients and your own reputation.

Tactic
What it looks like

Buying or selling links that pass ranking credit, large-scale link exchanges, automated link building

Paid links and sponsorship, done right

Paying for advertising or sponsored articles is normal business. The rule is about labelling. Google asks that links in paid or sponsored content carry **rel="sponsored"**, links you do not vouch for can carry **rel="nofollow"**, and links in comments or forums can carry **rel="ugc"** (user-generated content). If a blogger asks you for money for a "do-follow backlink", that is the link spam Google prohibits.

Earning links and mentions honestly
Join your trade association, market association or chamber of commerce and ask to be listed on its website.
Supply genuine expert comment or a useful local guide to Nigerian blogs and news sites that cover your field.
Sponsor or take part in community events that list partners online, and accept a sponsored label.
Create something worth linking to: a clear price guide, a how-to video, a free checklist.
Make sure suppliers, partners and event organisers who already mention you link to the right page.
Worked example: Turning down a risky offer
For example, Grace runs a small accounting firm in Port Harcourt. She receives a WhatsApp message offering "500 high-authority backlinks for N40,000, rank on page 1 in 30 days".
She checks Google's spam policies and confirms that buying links that pass ranking credit is listed as link spam.
She declines and instead lists the firm on her professional body's member directory, which links to her site.
She writes a practical article on filing deadlines for small businesses and shares it with two local business groups. A Port Harcourt business blog links to it.
She records the two new genuine links in her SEO sheet.
Two relevant, trusted links instead of 500 risky ones, and no chance of a manual action. She keeps the offer screenshot as an example for clients.

Be careful with fake or exaggerated claims too. Saying "NAFDAC approved" when a product is not registered, or inventing awards and customer numbers, misleads people and can break consumer protection rules as well as hurting trust. Only state what you can prove, and show registration numbers where they genuinely exist.
If a manual action arrives

Search Console shows any manual action under Security and Manual actions. Read the description, fix every issue it names (for example remove or label paid links), then submit a reconsideration request explaining what you changed. Do not ignore it.

Before agreeing to any link, ask one question: would I want this link even if Google did not exist? A listing on your market association's site sends real customers. A link from an unrelated foreign casino blog sends nobody, and exists only to fool a ranking system.
Inclusion and honesty

Good SEO overlaps with good accessibility. Alt text lets people using screen readers know what an image shows. Clear headings, plain words and readable font sizes help older visitors and those with less schooling. Where many customers prefer Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or Pidgin, a page in that language can serve them better. Be honest with clients too: give realistic timelines, report bad months as well as good, and never take credit for results caused by something else, such as a festive season peak.
Data privacy

Do not paste customer phone numbers or emails into public tools or AI chatbots. If a site collects personal data through forms, it should explain what it collects and why, in line with Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, and only people who need the data should see it.

Worked example: Finding a quick win
For example, Funke compares 3 months before and after her on-page changes to the birthday cakes page in Ibadan.
Before: 2,400 impressions, 48 clicks. CTR = 48 / 2,400 = 2 percent. Average position 14.
After: 5,100 impressions, 204 clicks. CTR = 204 / 5,100 = 4 percent. Average position 8.
In the Queries tab she sees "wedding cake price Ibadan" with 1,300 impressions but only 9 clicks, average position 7.
Her wedding page title is "Wedding". She rewrites it to "Wedding Cake Prices in Ibadan, Designs from Approx. N150,000 | Funke Cakes" and adds a clear price section.
She notes the date of the change in her sheet so she can check that query again in 6 weeks.
Clicks to the birthday page rose from 48 to 204 (more than four times). She also found a query that already had visibility but a weak title, the classic quick win.

Make one change

Wait 4 to 8 weeks

Change one thing at a time and give Google time to recrawl, so you know what worked.
Reading average position carefully

Average position is easy to misread. If your page ranks 3rd for one query and 40th for another, the average says 21.5, which describes neither. Always look at position per query, not only the site total. Also remember that a fall in average position can happen when you start appearing for many new searches at low positions. That is often good news: Google is testing your pages for more queries. Check impressions and clicks alongside it before you worry.

Search Console data usually arrives with a delay of a couple of days, and very rare queries are hidden to protect searchers' privacy, so totals in the Queries tab may not add up to the chart total. Both are normal.

Then filter by the channel **Organic Search** to see how many came from Google. Your Business Profile Performance view adds calls and direction requests. Many Nigerian customers order by WhatsApp, so also ask new customers "How did you find us?" and keep a simple tally.

Search demand changes with seasons (cakes in December, school uniforms in September), public holidays, news and Google updates. Always compare like with like, such as this November with last November, and mention seasonal effects in reports.

Before auditing someone else's business, get their agreement in writing (a WhatsApp message is fine) and ask them to add you as a Restricted user in Search Console and as a manager on the Business Profile. Never ask for passwords.

Test like a customer as well as a technician. On your own phone, search the business's main keyword, find it on Maps, open the website, and try to place an order or send a WhatsApp message. Note anything confusing: a phone number that does not connect, a menu that hides prices, a form that never confirms it was sent. These customer-journey problems belong in the audit too, because they decide whether search visibility turns into sales.

How Search Works
Three stages every page passes
Crawling: Googlebot visits pages through links
Indexing: Google understands and stores the page
Serving: Google shows the most useful matches
No crawl, no index. No index, no ranking.
Stage one is crawling. Google uses automatic programs called crawlers. Google's crawler is called Googlebot.
Crawlers find new pages mainly by following links, and from sitemaps, which are files that list a site's pages.
Stage two is indexing. Google reads the text, headings, images and title, and may store the page in its index, a huge database of pages.
Copies, very thin pages and pages with a noindex instruction are usually left out.
Stage three is serving results. When someone searches, Google returns the pages it thinks are most relevant and useful.
So remember this. A page can only rank after it has been crawled and indexed. A problem early in the flow blocks everything after it.

The audit order
Five parts of an SEO audit
Work in this order. An early problem makes later fixes useless.
An SEO audit is a structured check of how well a site and its Business Profile can be found, understood and chosen. It ends with a list of fixes in order.
First, indexing: is the site verified, the sitemap submitted, and are important pages in Google?
Second, technical health: secure HTTPS, mobile layout, page speed, broken links.
Third, on-page and content: unique titles, one H1, alt text, and helpful content for each keyword group.
Fourth, local presence: a verified profile, the right category, and the same name, address and phone everywhere.
Fifth, measurement and links. Always work in this order, because a page Google cannot index gains nothing from a better title.

Fix high-impact, easy issues first. These are your quick wins.
Record every issue in one row of a sheet, with evidence, impact, effort and the fix. An issue without evidence is only an opinion.

Do and don't when auditing
Do

Don't

Get the owner's agreement in writing first. A WhatsApp message is fine. Ask to be added as a Restricted user in Search Console and as a manager on the Business Profile.
Then test like a customer: search, open the site, and try to send a WhatsApp message.
Never ask for passwords. Look at competitors to explain your advice, never to copy them. Never promise rankings. And show the evidence without blaming anyone.

Owners want to know if SEO is worth it. Google says it usually takes four months to a year to show benefit, so share that early.
For example, Blessing reports to the furniture workshop after three months, using only figures the owner gives her.
Analytics shows 64 WhatsApp taps from Google search last month. The owner says about 1 in 8 chats becomes a sale. That is 8 sales. His average order is about 180,000 naira, so about 1,440,000 naira.
